copies/gpu: Training runs on GPUs, graphics processing units: the chips that do its multiplications, thousands at once. A large one holds eighty gigabytes.
copies/state: A model of seven billion parameters, trained with Adam, keeps sixteen bytes per parameter: a hundred and twelve gigabytes. That is more than one GPU holds.
copies/dp: Data parallelism shares the work among GPUs, say four, but gives each one a full copy of the weights, and so of the whole training state.
copies/waste: Between them, the four hold three hundred and twenty gigabytes, plenty for a hundred and twelve. Yet none can train the model: each must fit an identical copy on its own.
copies/idea: So keep a single copy, cut into four pieces, one per GPU: twenty eight gigabytes each, and it fits.
copies/shard: A broken-off piece of something, like glass, is called a shard, so this is called sharding.
copies/name: In 2019, Samyam Rajbhandari and colleagues at Microsoft named it zero, for Zero Redundancy Optimizer: it brings the redundant copies, the ones not needed, down to zero.
stages/bar: Inside a GPU's sixteen bytes per parameter: two for the 16-bit weight, two for its gradient, and twelve for Adam: the master copy, m and v.
stages/s1: Stage one cuts Adam's twelve bytes, the biggest part, into four. Each GPU keeps one quarter: three bytes.
stages/own: It updates only its own quarter of the weights. Then the GPUs swap their new quarters, so each has all the new weights again.
stages/s1b: With the weight and gradient whole, that is two, plus two, plus three: seven bytes per parameter.
stages/s1gb: Forty nine gigabytes per GPU: under eighty, so it fits.
stages/s2: Stage two cuts the gradients too: a GPU that updates one quarter of the weights only needs that quarter's averaged gradient.
stages/s2b: Only the weight's two bytes stay whole, and the other fourteen split four ways: five and a half bytes per parameter.
stages/s2gb: That is thirty eight and a half gigabytes per GPU.
stages/s3: Stage three cuts the weights as well: all sixteen bytes split four ways, four per parameter.
stages/s3gb: Twenty eight gigabytes per GPU: a quarter of the hundred and twelve.
stages/rule: With N parameters on G GPUs, that is sixteen N over G bytes each: G times less than a full copy.
stages/saved: So each GPU here saves a hundred and twelve, minus twenty eight: eighty four gigabytes.
cost/gather: Stage three has a price. To compute, a GPU needs all the weights, and it keeps only a quarter. So just before each piece is used, its keeper sends it to the others, and they drop it after.
cost/same: The arithmetic does not change: the same averaged gradient, the same step. Only where the numbers live.
cost/traffic: The cost is traffic. The paper counts it: stages one and two send no more between GPUs than plain data parallelism, and stage three about one and a half times as much.
cost/more: And the shares keep shrinking as GPUs are added: on sixty four of them, the seven billion parameters need one point seven five gigabytes each.
cost/trillion: That was the aim in the paper's title: a trillion parameters. Their sixteen thousand gigabytes of state, over one thousand and twenty four GPUs, come to about sixteen gigabytes each.
